title: Estimating: analytical, analogous, parametric & Delphi
blurb: Choose between analytical, analogous, parametric and Delphi estimating, use three-point ranges, and explain the estimating funnel.
question: A housing association must estimate replacing the windows in 400 homes. It has a cost per window from last year's contracts, a similar estate refurbished three years ago, and a heat-pump pilot nobody has done before. Which estimating method suits each, and why should the first figure be given as a range?

teach.h: An estimate is a forecast, not a promise
teach.body: An estimate is an informed approximation of the time, cost or resources needed for work, made before all the facts are known. It should always state its assumptions and, especially early on, be expressed as a range. Plain English: a best guess with its working shown. Different methods suit different stages, because what you know about the work changes as the project progresses.

rows.label: How
values: Bottom-up: estimate each WBS item, add up
Compare with a similar past project

rows.label: Watch out
values: Only as good as the data

teach.h: Which method fits what you have?
teach.caption: Methods are often combined: for example, parametric for repeatable items and analytical for the rest.

teach.h: Analytical: built from the bottom up
teach.body: Analytical (bottom-up) estimating breaks the scope down using the WBS, estimates each work package or activity, then adds them up. Because every piece is examined, it is the most accurate and gives a clear audit trail. The price is time and effort, and it needs a well-defined scope, so it is normally used later, from definition onwards, once the detail exists. Plain English: price every brick, then total the wall.

For the 400 homes, Coastline uses PARAMETRIC estimating: last year's contracts give a reliable cost per window, multiplied by the number of windows. For the refurbishment of a second estate, it uses ANALOGOUS estimating: it starts from the similar estate done three years ago and adjusts for size, inflation and access. For the heat-pump pilot, with no history, it runs a DELPHI exercise with external specialists.

steps.label: Share the summary
steps.sub: Facilitator feeds back range and reasons

teach.caption: Anonymity stops the most senior or loudest expert from dominating. It is not a group meeting or brainstorm.
Three-point estimating gives a range rather than a single figure, showing the uncertainty and where risk sits. The exam will not ask you to calculate with it.
Widths are illustrative, not APM figures. In iterative projects, near-term backlog items are estimated in detail and later items stay rough until they come closer.

teach.text: Analogous vs parametric is the classic mix-up. ANALOGOUS compares the whole job with a similar past project (and adjusts). PARAMETRIC uses a statistical unit rate multiplied by a quantity (cost per window × number of windows). And Delphi is ANONYMOUS rounds through a facilitator, not a workshop where experts debate face to face.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the method and say how it works (bottom-up, comparison, unit rate, anonymous rounds).
Say when it suits: analogous and parametric early; analytical once scope is detailed; Delphi for novel work.
Give one strength and one limitation of each method you discuss.
Explain that early estimates carry more uncertainty, so give a range (three-point) with assumptions.
Link to the estimating funnel: accuracy improves as information improves, so estimates are refined.
Analytical: bottom-up from the WBS; most accurate, but slow and needs detail.
Analogous: comparison with a similar past project; quick, adjust for differences.
Parametric: unit rate × quantity from reliable historical data.
Delphi: anonymous experts over several rounds with a facilitator, avoiding dominant voices.
Three-point (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic) gives a range; the funnel narrows as information improves.

summary: You can now explain how analytical, analogous, parametric and Delphi estimating work, when each suits and their strengths and limits. You can also explain why early estimates are ranges, how three-point estimating expresses that, and what the estimating funnel shows.

A.q: A project manager estimates every work package in the WBS and adds them up to produce the total. Which estimating method is this?
options: Analogous
Analytical
Parametric
Delphi
A.why: Building the estimate from the bottom up, item by item from the WBS, is analytical estimating.

whyNot.0: Analogous compares the whole project with a similar past one rather than building up from the WBS.
whyNot.2: Parametric multiplies a unit rate by a quantity.
whyNot.3: Delphi gathers anonymous expert estimates over several rounds.

A.q: An events company estimates a new conference by starting from the cost of a similar conference it ran last year. Which method is this?
options: Analytical
Parametric
Analogous
Three-point
A.why: Using a similar past project as the basis for the estimate is analogous (comparative) estimating.

whyNot.0: Analytical would build up the cost from every individual item.
whyNot.1: Parametric would apply a unit rate, such as cost per delegate, to a quantity.
whyNot.3: Three-point gives optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values, not a comparison with a past event.

A.q: A road maintenance team estimates resurfacing using a known cost per square metre multiplied by the area. Which method is this?
options: Parametric
Analogous
Delphi
Analytical
A.why: Applying a statistical unit rate (cost per square metre) to a quantity (the area) is parametric estimating.

whyNot.1: Analogous compares the job with a whole similar project rather than using a unit rate.
whyNot.2: Delphi uses anonymous expert judgement over several rounds.
whyNot.3: Analytical builds the estimate from every work package in the WBS.

B.q: Which feature is essential to the Delphi estimating technique?
options: A single expert gives a final figure
Experts debate face to face to agree
Anonymous experts revise over rounds
Historical unit rates are multiplied
B.why: Delphi collects estimates from experts anonymously, feeds back the results through a facilitator and repeats the rounds until a consensus emerges.

whyNot.0: Delphi relies on several experts, not one.
whyNot.1: Face-to-face debate is what Delphi avoids, because dominant voices can sway the group.
whyNot.3: Multiplying unit rates is parametric estimating.

B.q: Which three values are used in three-point estimating?
options: Minimum, average and maximum cost
Optimistic, most likely and pessimistic
Planned, earned and actual value
Analytical, analogous and parametric
B.why: Three-point estimating uses an optimistic, a most likely and a pessimistic value to give a range that reflects uncertainty.

whyNot.0: These sound similar but are not the three named points of the technique.
whyNot.2: Planned, earned and actual value are earned value measures.
whyNot.3: These are estimating methods, not the three points of a three-point estimate.

B.q: Why is analytical estimating normally used later in a linear life cycle rather than at concept?
options: It needs a detailed scope and WBS first
It is the least accurate of the methods
It can only be used for cost, not time
It requires anonymous expert panels
B.why: Analytical estimating builds up from the WBS, so it needs the scope defined in detail. That detail usually only exists from definition onwards.

whyNot.1: It is usually the most accurate method, not the least.
whyNot.2: It can be used for time, cost and resources.

C.q: A charity needs a quick early estimate for a community hub. It built a very similar hub in another town two years ago, but the new site is larger. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Bottom-up from a full WBS before any figure
Use the past hub's cost without adjustment
Delphi rounds, since nothing similar exists
Analogous, adjusted for the size difference
C.why: A similar past project makes analogous estimating quick and suitable at this early stage, provided it is adjusted for known differences such as size.

whyNot.0: A full WBS isn't available yet, and the charity needs a quick early figure.
whyNot.1: Failing to adjust for scale and other differences produces a misleading estimate.
whyNot.2: Something similar does exist, so Delphi's strength with novel work isn't needed.

C.q: In estimating workshops for a new technology, the most senior engineer's views always prevail and others stay silent. Which method would best counter this?
options: Parametric
Analogous
Delphi
Analytical
C.why: Delphi keeps experts' estimates anonymous and routes feedback through a facilitator, so no single dominant voice can sway the result. It also suits novel technology with little historical data.

whyNot.0: Parametric needs reliable historical unit data, which new technology lacks, and does not address group dynamics.
whyNot.1: Analogous needs a similar past project and does not deal with dominant voices.
whyNot.3: Analytical needs detailed scope and could still be dominated by the senior engineer.

C.q: Which statement about the estimating funnel is NOT correct?
options: Estimate ranges narrow as information improves
Accuracy is greatest at the concept stage
Early estimates rest heavily on assumptions
Estimates are refined through the life cycle
C.why: Accuracy is lowest at concept, when least is known. It improves as the project progresses and more information becomes available.

whyNot.0: This is correct: the range narrows as uncertainty reduces.
whyNot.2: This is correct: early estimates depend on assumptions that must be recorded and validated.
whyNot.3: This is correct: estimates are revisited and refined as the project moves forward.

reteach.title: Think of a house extension
reteach.question: You want to know what a single-storey extension will cost. A neighbour built one, builders quote per square metre, and your architect can price every item once the drawings are done. Which is which?

blocks.h: Four ways to price your extension
blocks.body: Asking your neighbour what theirs cost, then allowing for yours being bigger, is ANALOGOUS. A builder's 'about £X per square metre' times your floor area is PARAMETRIC. The quantity surveyor pricing every brick, joist and socket from the final drawings is ANALYTICAL. Asking three surveyors to estimate separately, sharing the spread, and letting them revise without knowing whose figure is whose is DELPHI.

blocks.text: The neighbour's whole job is ANALOGOUS. The rate per square metre is PARAMETRIC. Don't swap them.

explain.body: Bottom-up: estimate each item in the WBS and total them. Most accurate and traceable, but time-consuming and only possible when the scope is defined in detail.

test.q: What is the main drawback of analytical estimating?
options: It ignores the work breakdown structure
It takes time and needs detailed scope
It relies on one past project's figures
It hides the basis of the final estimate
test.why: Analytical estimating examines every item, so it is slow and needs a well-defined scope and WBS before it can be done.

whyNot.0: It is built directly from the WBS.
whyNot.2: Relying on a past project describes analogous estimating.
whyNot.3: It is the most traceable method, because every item is visible.

explain.body: Analogous compares the job with a similar past project and adjusts for differences. Parametric applies a statistical unit rate to a quantity. Both are quick and suit early stages; parametric needs reliable data and work that scales in a predictable way.

test.q: Parametric estimating is only reliable when which condition is met?
options: A panel of experts agrees anonymously
Every work package is fully specified
No similar project has ever been done
Historical unit data is accurate and scales
test.why: Parametric estimating multiplies a unit rate by a quantity, so it depends on accurate historical data and work that scales predictably.

whyNot.1: Full specification of every work package is what analytical estimating needs.
whyNot.2: Parametric needs history; a lack of precedent points towards Delphi.

explain.body: Experts estimate independently and anonymously. A facilitator collects the estimates, shares the range and reasoning, and asks for revised estimates. Rounds repeat until the estimates converge, so no dominant voice sways the outcome.

test.q: What is the facilitator's role in a Delphi estimate?
options: To collate and feed back the anonymous estimates
To choose the most senior expert's estimate
To chair a debate until the panel agrees
To apply unit rates to the agreed quantities
test.why: The facilitator gathers each round of anonymous estimates, shares the summary and reasons, and runs further rounds until consensus.

whyNot.1: Choosing the senior expert's figure is exactly the bias Delphi avoids.
whyNot.2: Delphi avoids face-to-face debate to prevent dominant voices.
whyNot.3: Applying unit rates is parametric estimating.

explain.body: Early estimates carry more uncertainty, so present a range with assumptions. Three-point estimating (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic) expresses it. The estimating funnel shows the range narrowing as information improves.

test.q: A sponsor asks for one exact figure at concept stage. Why is a range a better answer?
options: Ranges avoid the need for any assumptions
Ranges stay the same width all through
Single figures are banned by governance
A range reflects the real uncertainty now
test.why: At concept little is known, so a range (with its assumptions) honestly shows the uncertainty. It narrows as information improves.

whyNot.0: Ranges still rest on assumptions, which should be stated.
whyNot.1: Ranges narrow over the life cycle, as the estimating funnel shows.
whyNot.2: There is no such rule; the issue is giving a false sense of certainty.
